title: Data Decisions and Theoretical Implications when Adversarially Learning Fair Representations
abstract: How can we learn a classifier that is "fair" for a protected or sensitive group, when we do not know if the input to the classifier belongs to the protected group? How can we train such a classifier when data on the protected group is difficult to attain? In many settings, finding out the sensitive input attribute can be prohibitively expensive even during model training, and sometimes impossible during model serving. For example, in recommender systems, if we want to predict if a user will click on a given recommendation, we often do not know many attributes of the user, e.g., race or age, and many attributes of the content are hard to determine, e.g., the language or topic. Thus, it is not feasible to use a different classifier calibrated based on knowledge of the sensitive attribute. Here, we use an adversarial training procedure to remove information about the sensitive attribute from the latent representation learned by a neural network. In particular, we study how the choice of data for the adversarial training effects the resulting fairness properties. We find two interesting results: a small amount of data is needed to train these adversarial models, and the data distribution empirically drives the adversary's notion of fairness.

claims.text: Training the adversarial head on data containing both positive and negative target label classes (Y=1 and Y=0) theoretically enforces demographic parity in predictions.
Training the adversarial head exclusively on positive target class instances (Y=1) theoretically enforces equality of opportunity for the positive class.
Training the adversarial head exclusively on negative target class instances (Y=0) theoretically enforces equality of opportunity for the negative class.
Using a balanced distribution over the sensitive attribute in adversarial training stabilizes model performance and reduces variance across training runs.
Using a balanced sensitive attribute distribution in adversarial training improves fairness metrics across all tested measures compared to an unbalanced distribution.
Using a balanced sensitive attribute distribution in adversarial training decreases primary task classification accuracy.
Training the adversarial head on high-income examples (>50K) most effectively reduces the equality gap for the high-income label class.
Training the adversarial head on low-income examples (<=50K) most effectively reduces the equality gap for the low-income label class.
Adversarial fair representation learning remains effective at improving fairness metrics with sensitive attribute datasets as small as 500 examples (1.5% of total training data).

limitations.text: Post-processing calibration methods for fairness require observing the sensitive attribute during model serving, which is infeasible when attributes are unobservable or expensive to obtain.
Prior adversarial debiasing approaches do not analyze or specify the effect of limited or skewed training data distributions on the fairness definition being optimized.
Enforcing unbiased latent representations directly inside the model acts as a strong constraint that significantly degrades overall classification accuracy.

methodologies.name: Adversarial Fair Representation Learning with Data Distribution Variant S
methodologies.description: A multi-head deep neural network architecture where one head predicts the primary target label and an adversarial head predicts the sensitive attribute via a negative gradient layer to remove sensitive information from the shared hidden embedding.
conditions: Logistic loss for primary and adversarial heads
Adagrad optimizer with step size 0.01 for 100,000 steps
Evaluated across varying sensitive attribute balance (balanced vs unbalanced)
Evaluated across varying target label distributions (low income, high income, equal balance)
Evaluated across adversarial dataset sizes (500, 1000, 2000, 4000 examples)
